title: Procurement Basics
summary: Learn how public and organisational procurement works: principles of value for money and fairness, the procurement cycle and specifications, procurement methods and thresholds, bid evaluation with worked scoring, contract management and whole-life cost, and integrity, red flags and tips for suppliers. Calculations were checked in code.
audience: Procurement and finance officers, small business owners bidding for contracts, and public sector staff

lessons.title: What procurement is and why it matters

body.p: Procurement is the process of buying goods, services and works, from pens and medicines to computer systems, consultants and roads. In the public sector it often accounts for a large share of government spending, so how it is done affects whether money delivers schools, clinics and infrastructure or is wasted or stolen.

list: Value for money: the best combination of cost, quality and whole-life benefit, not simply the lowest price.
Fairness and equal treatment of suppliers.
Transparency: open advertising, clear criteria and published awards.
Competition: enough suppliers bidding to get good prices.
Accountability: decisions recorded and open to audit and review.
Integrity: no conflicts of interest, bribes or favouritism.

body.p: Public procurement is governed by procurement laws and regulations, and often by constitutional principles. Many countries also use procurement to support local businesses and historically disadvantaged groups.

body.tip: Procurement is not just a paperwork function; it is one of the most powerful tools an organisation has to achieve its goals.

steps: Identify the need and check the budget.
Plan: decide what to buy, the method and the timeline, and include it in the annual procurement plan.
Write specifications or terms of reference.
Evaluate bids against the published criteria.
Award the contract and notify bidders.
Manage the contract: delivery, quality checks, payments and variations.
Close out and review lessons learned.

body.p: Good specifications describe what is needed (function, performance and standards), not a particular brand, so more suppliers can compete. Vague specifications lead to poor-quality goods; overly narrow ones can be used to favour one supplier.

A school needs 120 desks at an estimated R250 each: 120 x 250 = R30 000. Adding 15% VAT of R4500 gives R34 500. Accurate estimates help choose the right procurement method and detect unrealistic bids.

body.tip: Plan procurement early in the financial year; rushed purchases at year-end are a common source of waste.

list: Open competitive bidding (open tender): advertised publicly; anyone qualified can bid. The default for large purchases.
Restricted or selective bidding: only prequalified suppliers are invited, for specialised needs.
Request for quotations: for lower-value purchases, usually at least three written quotes.
Direct procurement or single sourcing: only in limited, justified cases such as emergencies or when only one supplier exists; it carries a high risk of abuse.
Framework agreements: pre-agreed terms with suppliers for repeated purchases.
Two-stage bidding for complex projects.

body.p: Laws set value thresholds that determine which method must be used. Splitting a large purchase into smaller orders to stay under a threshold and avoid competition is a common irregularity and is usually prohibited.
Online portals publish tenders, receive bids and record decisions, improving transparency and reducing opportunities for manipulation. Many African governments now publish tenders and awards online.

body.tip: Always document why a particular method was used, especially for direct procurement.

body.p: Bids are evaluated only against the criteria published in the bid documents, usually in stages.

steps: Administrative compliance: required forms, tax clearance and registration.
Technical or functionality evaluation: experience, methodology, staff and quality, often with a minimum score.
Preference points or margins where the law provides them.

body.p: Some systems use a formula such as points = 80 x (1 - (Pt - Pmin) / Pmin), where Pt is the bid price and Pmin the lowest acceptable price. The lowest bid of R1 000 000 scores 80; a bid of R1 100 000 scores 72; R1 250 000 scores 60.
With 70% for quality and 30% for price, a bid scoring 85 on quality and 70 on price gets 0.7 x 85 + 0.3 x 70 = 80.5, beating a cheaper bid scoring 70 on quality and 100 on price (79.0).

body.tip: Evaluation committee members must declare conflicts of interest and step aside where they have one.

body.p: Awarding the contract is the start, not the end. Many failures happen during delivery.

list: Contracts should state scope, price, delivery dates, quality standards, payment terms, penalties for delay, dispute resolution and termination.
Inspect and accept goods against the specification before payment.
Track milestones and keep records of meetings and instructions.
Control variations: changes to scope or price must be justified and approved; large variations can be a sign of manipulation.
Pay suppliers on time; late payment harms small businesses.

body.p: Compare total cost of ownership, not just price. A machine costing R50 000 with R5000 a year of maintenance over five years costs R75 000; one costing R60 000 with R2000 a year costs R70 000, making the more expensive purchase cheaper over its life.

body.tip: Keep a contract register listing every contract, its value, dates and responsible manager.

body.h: Red flags of corruption and fraud

list: Specifications that only one supplier can meet.
Very short bidding periods or poor advertising.
Bidders with shared addresses, directors or phone numbers (possible collusion).
Repeated awards to the same supplier or splitting of orders.
Large variations soon after award.
Officials with undeclared links to suppliers.

body.p: Protections include segregation of duties, rotation of committee members, publishing awards, independent bid appeals or review boards, debarment of fraudulent suppliers, and whistle-blowing channels.

Register on government supplier databases, keep tax and company documents current, read bid documents fully, attend briefing sessions, answer every requirement and submit before the deadline. Late or incomplete bids are usually rejected without being evaluated.

body.tip: Small businesses can start with low-value quotations to build a track record before larger tenders.

options: The best mix of cost, quality and whole-life benefit
Function and performance, not a brand
